lesson.title: Matched Pairs: Blocks of Exactly Two
lesson.summary: A matched pairs design is a special case of block design in which subjects are grouped into pairs that are similar on key traits, or a single subject serves as their own pair across two conditions, with assignment randomized within each pair.
lesson.body:
A matched pairs design takes the logic of randomized block design and shrinks the block size down to two. Instead of grouping many subjects who share a trait, researchers form pairs, either two similar subjects matched on relevant characteristics, or a single subject who experiences both treatments and effectively serves as their own match. Within each pair, which member gets which treatment, or which treatment comes first, is decided at random. Because each pair already controls for whatever traits made its two members alike, matched pairs designs can detect smaller treatment effects with fewer subjects than an unmatched comparison would need.

There are two common versions. In the first, researchers recruit subjects in twos, matching each pair on traits expected to affect the outcome, twins, siblings, or two patients of similar age and baseline health, then randomly decide which twin gets the new treatment and which gets the standard one. In the second, a single subject provides both data points: each person tries both treatments, usually in a randomly chosen order, and the two results are compared within that same person. This second version is sometimes called a within-subjects or repeated-measures design, but it is still a matched pairs design because the pair is one person's two measurements rather than two different people.

Consider a hypothetical taste test comparing two recipes for a granola bar. Researchers recruit 30 volunteers and give each volunteer both recipes, Recipe A and Recipe B, on two separate days, randomly deciding for each volunteer whether they taste Recipe A or Recipe B first, then rate each on a 10-point scale. Because the same person rates both recipes, personal differences in how generously people give ratings, one volunteer might rate everything a 9, another might rate everything a 5, cancel out when the researcher looks at each volunteer's difference score, Recipe A minus Recipe B, rather than comparing the raw average ratings of two separate groups. Randomizing the tasting order guards against a further confound: order effects, where whichever recipe is tasted first might get an edge from novelty or a disadvantage from a fresher aftertaste lingering into the second taste.

The random assignment inside each pair remains essential, exactly as it is in the broader randomized block design. Without it, a researcher who always gave Recipe A first, or always assigned the healthier-looking twin to the new treatment, would reintroduce the very systematic bias that blocking and randomization together are meant to prevent. What makes matched pairs distinctive is not that randomization disappears, but that the block size is as small as it can possibly be, one matched unit, which maximizes the similarity between what is being compared within each block.

Matched pairs designs work best when a good matching variable, or a genuine repeated-measures setup, is available and practical; they are less useful when subjects cannot be sensibly paired or when trying both treatments on the same subject would carry over effects from one condition into the other, for instance a subject who improves permanently after treatment A cannot then serve as an unaffected baseline for treatment B. When those conditions are met, though, matched pairs is often the most statistically efficient design available, squeezing more information out of a smaller sample than an unblocked, unmatched comparison could.
